evidence.title: Benefit-Risk Reporting for FDA-Cleared Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices
evidence.outcome: Postmarket adverse events and recalls among AI/ML devices
evidence.effect: 489 adverse events involving 36 (5.2%) devices, including 458 malfunctions, 30 injuries, 1 death; 40 devices (5.8%) recalled 113 times, mostly software issues.
evidence.quote: A total of 40 devices (5.8%) were recalled 113 times, primarily due to software issues.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether health system reporting of AI adverse events or cross-site sharing of lessons reduces harm, so support rests on 13 endorsements and one descriptive study showing that FDA-cleared AI devices generate adverse events and recalls. Systems may adopt reporting to meet existing FDA and state obligations, but its value for detecting systemic hazards across sites remains unproven.

perspectives.view: No study tests whether reporting AI adverse events or sharing de-identified lessons with peer sites speeds recognition of systemic hazards or reduces harm. One descriptive study of 691 FDA-cleared devices documents the hazard, which is indirect evidence for the practice. The 13 endorsing sources are mostly frameworks and commentaries, and they reflect expert judgment rather than tested outcomes.

The FDA database analysis recorded 489 adverse events across 36 (5.2%) devices, including 458 malfunctions, 30 injuries, and 1 death, along with 113 recalls of 40 devices, mostly for software issues. These counts suggest that failures surface after clearance. Passive reports may undercount events, and the study does not show that more reporting catches errors before they reach patients.

The FDA draft guidance states that manufacturers must report deaths and serious injuries, and New York already requires reporting of certain adverse events through NYPORTS. In these sources, health system submission to patient safety organizations and sharing with peer sites remains voluntary. Several commentaries call for mandatory reporting or a national AI clinical decision support safety clearinghouse.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare sites with and without structured AI adverse event reporting and peer sharing. Useful outcomes include time to detection of a systemic hazard, time to vendor fix or recall, and repeat events at other sites. Studies should also measure how completely voluntary reports capture AI-related harms when checked against chart review.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The single hazard study used national FDA device data and did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. It is therefore unknown whether current reporting channels capture AI harms in these groups, where events may be less often recognized or reported.
